summary: Lists general requirements in support of Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS). It does not present solutions, and additional requirements for specific applications are to be specified in separate documents. It is informational.

eli5.summary: During a disaster, important calls from rescuers must get through. This lists what a network must be able to do to help, without saying how to build it yet.

questions: emergency communications priority on the internet
what is ets emergency telecommunications service
what are the ets general requirements
why keep policy separate from labels
does ets guarantee better than best effort
subtitle: A short list of what the Internet must be able to do so that authorized emergency traffic can be told apart and given a better chance.

tldr.problem: After a disaster, responders need quick access to public telecommunications, which are increasingly Internet based. The Internet community needs to decide how it can best support emergency management and recovery operations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists general requirements: labels that mark emergency traffic, optional signaling to carry them, policy kept separate from labels, probabilistic better-than-best-effort treatment, and authorization, authentication and confidentiality. It gives no solutions.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational blueprint. More specific requirements, such as those for IP telephony in RFC 3690, are meant to build on it in separate documents.

today: RFC 3689 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the general requirements document for ETS, and its IP telephony companion is RFC 3690.

sections.title: Why Emergency Service Matters
sections.content:
RFC 3689 opens with the observation that effective telecommunications can be imperative for recovery after serious disasters such as hurricanes, floods, earthquakes and terrorist attacks. Responders need immediate access to whatever public capabilities are at hand: telephones, cellular phones, and Internet access through terminals, IP telephones and wireless PDAs.

Because the commercial infrastructure is evolving toward Internet-based technology, the document says the Internet community needs to consider how it can best support emergency management. The result is Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS), described through a list of general requirements.
sections.eli5: If a storm knocks things down, helpers need to talk to each other. More and more of that talking happens over the Internet, so the Internet should be ready to help.

sections.title: Existing Emergency Standards and the Problem
sections.content:
The RFC lists emergency standards from other organizations: T1.631 from ANSI, and E.106, F.706, H.460.4 and I.255.3 from the ITU. T1.631 defines an indicator for SS7 networks that signals a need for High Probability of Completion service, and is the basis for the U.S. Government Emergency Telecommunications Service (GETS). Most of these standards cover telephony or define telephony-related labels. They are outside the IETF's scope but serve as examples of ETS.

The problem for the IEPREP working group is how, and to what degree, such support fits into the Internet architecture and existing IETF standards. The requirements must not focus only on IP telephony. The Japanese I-Am-Alive (IAA) database is an example of a non-telephony ETS application: people register and query status after an event such as an earthquake, and signaling like SIP is not always needed. So solutions must not assume signaling and must work for applications that only have labels in data packets, in places such as the application or IP header.
sections.eli5: Phone companies already have ways to mark urgent calls. But not everything is a phone call. A website where people say they are safe also matters, so the plan has to cover more than phones.

sections.title: Scope and What Is Left Out
sections.content:
The document defines general system requirements for ETS, drawing on GETS (signaled, interactive, non-elastic applications) and IAA (non-signaled, elastic applications). It stresses that ETS is not the only way to support authorized emergency communications, only an approach shaped by existing systems and standards.

It defines no solutions and specifies no protocol changes. Requirements for specific application types go in other documents, and the IEPREP charter says proposed solutions are developed in other working groups. Out of scope are emulating specific architectures such as the PSTN, focusing on one application, and requirements aimed at government regulations or laws. Mandating that anyone support the requirements is also out of scope: the document expects business contracts such as Service Level Agreements to cover providers, and says that without an SLA, best effort service is provided.
sections.eli5: This paper only says what is needed. It does not build anything, and it cannot force anyone to follow it. Companies would agree on it in contracts.

sections.title: The General Requirements
sections.content:
Four general requirements come first.

  • Signaling: IF signaling is used to convey the state or existence of an emergency, then signaling mechanisms MUST exist to carry the applicable labels.
  • Labels: labels may exist in various forms at different layers, in signaling and/or in a data packet header. Labels from different layers are NOT required to be the same, but MAY be related.
  • Policy: policy MUST be kept separate from labels. The mechanism used to achieve a characteristic MUST NOT be stated in the label definition, and interaction between unrelated labels MUST NOT be embedded in a label. Local policy decides such things.
  • Network functionality: better-than-best-effort support SHOULD focus on probability rather than guarantees, such as reduced packet loss, minimal jitter or minimal end-to-end delay. There is no requirement that such functionality exist, or be ubiquitous between end users.

A label here is simply an identifier, such as a numeric value or a bit pattern in a packet header. The RFC cites the Assured Forwarding bit pattern of RFC 2597 as an example of a label that does not involve routing.
sections.eli5: Mark urgent mail with a sticker. The sticker says only that it is urgent, not how the post office must handle it. Each post office decides that itself, and nobody promises the mail will always be faster.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Open Issues
sections.content:
Three security requirements follow from the first four.

  • Authorization: only authorized users may have access to emergency services. Mechanisms beyond closed private networks SHOULD meet IETF Security Area criteria, so clear-text passwords would generally not be acceptable. They SHOULD be flexible enough for various levels of restriction.
  • Integrity and authentication: authorized emergency traffic needs reduced risk from denial of service, which implies protecting its integrity. Users SHOULD consider end-to-end integrity and authentication rather than relying on a single provider.
  • Confidentiality: a service MAY offer confidentiality options. Users SHOULD deploy end-to-end security and weigh alternatives such as PGP, TLS and IPsec transport-mode at different layers.

The RFC also lists issues, which are not requirements. Accounting is not a general requirement, but solutions should not preclude it. Labels distinguish emergency flows but do not create the ability to admit flows selectively, and schemes that rely on admission control will fail outside very controlled environments. Verifying digital signatures is computationally expensive, so a flood of invalid labelled traffic could be a denial-of-service attack, and systems that require such validation SHOULD define operational and protocol measures against it.
sections.eli5: Only the right people should be allowed to use the fast lane, and a fake pass should not work. Checking passes takes effort, so bad guys might try to jam the checkers with fake ones.

sections.title: Related Work
sections.content: The RFC points to RFC 3487, which describes requirements for resource priority mechanisms for the Session Initiation Protocol. That RFC covers one application-level protocol, while RFC 3689 is a generalization that is not application specific. It acts as a blueprint from which more specific requirements may be written, and the text notes that RFC 3690 was written for IP telephony.
sections.eli5: This paper is the general rulebook. Other papers can add extra rules for particular things, such as phone calls over the Internet.
